chapter: Los Angeles, Central Avenue and the Apex
title: Dr. Somerville and the Dunbar Hotel
summary: The Dunbar (formerly the Somerville) was built from the ground up by black physician Dr. Somerville in 1925-26, with the La Vada Apartments named for his wife.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: What about the hotel that later was the Dunbar that first was the Somerville?
The Dunbar -- the ground was broken there in 1925-26 area --
And that was black-owned, was it not? (inaudible)?

-- and it was black-owned by a very prominent physician, Dr. Somerville (PHONETIC). He saved up his money and without a whole lot of outside financing, he built the Dunbar Hotel and it was a first-class hotel. He also, about a half-mile away from there, put up the following year an apartment house called the La Vada Apartments, which was named after his wife, whose name was Vada (PHONETIC) Somerville. They were two of the nicest buildings on the East Side of town. At that time, that was the -- one of the first and only black hotels that had ever been built from the bottom up by blacks and it was the finest one in the United States.
Usually, when blacks got hotels is because the whites
that wanted out and then sold it to the blacks and they came into it. But this was built from the ground-breaking up, as a black corporation, I guess.
Well, before the Somerville was built, who traveled to Los Angeles? where could black people stay (inaudible)?
Most people that came to Los Angeles, when they came here, they went to rooming houses and to the homes of friends and stayed. There wasn't a black hotel in town that was first-class.
The Somerville, which became the Dunbar, 43rd about, is on Central Avenue, just North of Vernon (PHONETIC), (inaudible), right?
